 Twins News & Analysis 
 Unpopular Opinion: I Will Bet on Royce Lewis 
 Not only should the Twins tender a 2027 contract to Royce Lewis, but they should also work with him on an extension. 
 By 
 Seth Stohs 
 8 hours ago 
 Image courtesy of Jesse Johnson-Imagn Images via Reuters Connect
 Twins Video
 By 4:00 Minnesota time on Friday, we will find out which Twins players have been tendered a contract for the 2027 season. Nine Twins are arbitration-eligible, and there are a couple of fairly difficult decisions that may need to be made. 
 Reading opinion articles at Twins Daily and other sites, there is some thought that the Twins could just non-tender infielder Royce Lewis. MLB Trade Rumors projected Lewis to receive $5.1 million in 2027, his third of four years of arbitration-eligibility. 
 There is no way around it. 2026 was a very disappointing for Royce Lewis. The low point, most likely, was being optioned to St. Paul with no timeline for a comeback. In mid-May, his batting average was hovering around .160. At-bats were difficult to watch. So many check swings and lack of balance. As we know, he went to the Saints and played in 13 games. He hit .340/.417/.868 (1.285) with four doubles, eight homers and 19 RBI. He turned 27 while playing for St. Paul. A day later, he returned to the Twins and James Outman was DFAd. In 94 games after his return, he hit .245/.295/.409 (.704) with 21 doubles, 12 homers and 44 RBI. 
 Overall, he played in 125 games with the Twins in 2026. He hit .227/.287/.380 (.667) with 24 doubles, 15 home runs and 16 RBI. He was worth 0.9 bWAR and 0.5 fWAR. It was hit career-high in games played. He generally was healthy most of the season. In 2025, he had hit .237/.283/.388 (.671) with 18 doubles, 13 homers and 12 stolen bases in 106 games. The 667 and .671 OPS were 15% and 14% below league average, respectively. 
 Players within the 25 MLB hitters just ahead and 25 immediately following Lewis's .667 OPS in 2026 (minimum 350 PA) include Dansby Swanson (.694), Christian Yelich (.692), Matt Chapman (.692), Jose Ramirez (.688), Vlad Guerrero (.687), Xander Bogaerts (.676), Trea Turner (.675), Cal Raleigh (.664), Salvador Perez (.656), Austin Riley (.654), Dalton Varsho (.637), and Jarren Duran (.627). This group includes a few veterans who may be approaching the end of their career. Several of these players had injuries. Researchers will be researching for years what happened to Guerrero in 2026. But another thing you'll notice is that most of these guys still provide strong defense at their respective positions. Lewis certainly wouldn't qualify as Gold Glove caliber and moved from third base to first base when he returned from the minor leagues.  
 So yes, I can see that it was disappointing season. I know I could go more and add flames to the fire, but I'm not going to do that. Many already have written such things. When it comes to the stats, I won't put up too much of an argument. When people start throwing out personal issues they may have, or talk about him being hurt, or getting upset at quotes that he has made, then I'll roll my eyes and disagree. 
 Riding with Royce 
 So yeah, I'm going another direction than most with Royce Lewis. I'm betting on Lewis by offering a long-term contract with options. Think about what a long-term deal with Lewis would have looked like if he had signed something after his 2023 season when he hit .309 (.921) with 15 homers and 52 RBI in 58 games. He would have received a deal of at least eight years and probably $80-100 million. 
 This long-term deal idea will be much smaller than that. It will consider his struggles the last couple of years, but it also acknowledges his talent and upside and power potential that we do see from time to time throughout the season. It is a fairly short deal, with a reasonable base salary and some incentives similar to those included in Byron Buxton's contract signed in November 2021, just weeks before the last owners' lockout. (Reminder: Buxton signed a seven-year, $100 million contract in which he got $9 million for his final arbitration season and then six years with a base salary of $15 million. It then included incentives that were based on playing time (plate appearances) and performance MVP voting.) 
 Here is what my offer looks like: 
 Primary Offer 
 Signing Bonus: $1 million
 2027 (age 28): $5 million 
 2028 (age 29): $7.5 million
 2029 (age 30): $7.5 million. 
 Summary: The offer begins as a three-year, $22 million deal with a $1 million buyout (with a mutual option).
 Twins Club Option  
 Option A: If the Twins Decline their Option:  Buyout: $1 million.
 Option B: If the Twins Accept their Option:  
 2030 (age 31): $15 million
 2031 (age 32): $15 million
 Summary: After the three seasons, the Twins can choose to pick up a two-year, $30 million option. If things don't go as well, the Twins can decline the two-year option and pay Lewis a $1 million buyout. Along with getting the $1 million buyout, Lewis will have an option to stay with the Twins. 
 Player Option  
 If the Twins Decline their Option:  Lewis receives the $1 million Buyout and has an option of his own.
 Option A: Lewis accepts the one-year
 2030 (age 31): $5 million 
 Summary: Lewis may be an All Star in 2028 and 2029, but the Twins could still decline the two-year option for 2030 and 2031 and give Lewis the $1 million buyout. Instead of becoming a free agent coming off those two All Star seasons, Lewis could be so happy to have had all this time with the Twins and love the fans and his teammates so much that he wants to stay for one year at $8 million. OK, that scenario may not play out. More likely, 
 The Incentives 
 Plate Appearances: $250,000 for reaching 500, 525, 550, 575, 600, and 625 plate appearances. (annual maximum = $1.5 million)         
 Achievements: $4 million for MVP, $3.5 million for second in MVP voting, $3.0 million for third, $2.5 million for fourth, $2.5 million for fifth, and $1.5 million. Obviously, he could only get one of those bonuses per year. In addition, he would earn $1 million for each Silver Slugger and Gold Glove award he wins.)
 You will notice these are the same incentives found in Byron Buxton's contract, though generally about half the dollar amount. 
 The Contract Summary
 Guaranteed: 3 years, $21 million.
 Maximum 2027-2029 incentives: up to $7.5 million per year. 
 Guaranteed 2027-2029 maximum of 3 years, $43.5 million. 
 If Twins exercise the Club option, he would make $29 million for 2030 and 2031. plus, up to $7.5 million per year in incentives. 
 Five year guaranteed/option salary total: $50 million before incentives.
 If Twins decline option, the Twins would pay him a $1 million buyout. Lewis would have the ability to choose a one year, $8 million deal for 2030. In that scenario, he would make four years and $30 million (assuming that he'd accept the one-year deal and didn't earn much in incentives). 
 Why Lewis and Even Boras Might Consider This Deal? 
 Both are smart, logical thinkers who have to know that the luster and shine of his draft and prospect status have faded. They can't look at his stats the last three seasons and think of a 10-figure contract. He's already turned 27, so it's likely that a contract for eight of more years is very unlikely. With two seasons of arbitration remaining, is it more likely that he breaks out, or what might the odds be that two years from now, he's looking at minor-league offers with spring training invites? Lewis and Boras can say, MLB Trade Rumors projects you at $5.1 million. Right now, that's the only guaranteed money that you have (assuming the Twins tender the deal). With my proposal idea (or structure), there is $21 million in guaranteed money with incentives that can nearly double that number and an option that if picked up would then guarantee another $30 million and still have those same incentives. I might argue that it'd be silly if Lewis and Boras didn't strongly consider this type of deal. Even the $5 million isn't guaranteed if time is missed due to the impending owners' lockout. 
 Why Lewis and Boras Might Not Consider This Deal?
 You don't hire Scott Boras as an agent if you don't want to maximize your potential earnings. Maximizing the compensation would mean giving Lewis the chance to earn a bunch more money in his fourth and final arbitration-eligible offseason in a year. he can do that by putting up numbers in 2027. Maybe he does enough to warrant $10 million in 2028, and then he has another huge season in 2028 and becomes a 29-year-old free agent coming off of two strong years. That could make him $50-80 million, or at least something similar to what Ryan Jeffers could have received in free agency without the Qualifying Offer albatross. Or the Twins could offer that Qualifying Offer to Lewis. By then it's $25 million for that year. Now he will have made $40 million over these same three years and then can enter free agency as a 30-year-old. Frankly, it is up to Royce Lewis. He has to find a way to adjust at the plate and become more consistent. He can't have another sub-.300 OBP or sub .700 OPS. He has to find a defensive position that works for him. Maybe that's second base. I'd personally just put him at first base and play him every day that he can. I'd have Joe Mauer and Justin Morneau work with him all spring training and maybe even in-season.. 
 Why the Twins Would Consider Making This Deal?
 First, they would have some cost certainty. Second, this organization made him the #1 overall pick a decade ago. They've invested a lot of time and money to him, beyond his original signing bonus. If they are hanging on to any belief in what Lewis can be, post ACL surgeries, then this type of minimal short-term extension will show that to Lewis. As for the incentives, like with Buxton, if Lewis reaches those incentives they will be thrilled to pay the bonus dollars. If you believe that 1.0 WAR is worth $8-10 million. According to FanGraphs, Lewis has been "worth" $21.4 million over the past three seasons when he accumulated a total of 2.6 fWAR. If he's just worth what FanGraphs says he's been worth the last three seasons over the next three seasons, it will be disappointing. If he is the 2.3 fWAR player that he was in about a half a season in 2023, he'd justify the contract with one season. That's not unrealistic.  
 Why the Twins Might Not Consider Making This Deal? 
 I mean, they have a pretty solid analytics department that can look at the stats. The stats scream "Go year-to-year" at this point. Trading him now isn't ideal as you'd be trading so low. 
 What do you think? First, should the Twins tender Lewis a 2027 contract this afternoon? Should they non-tender him? Should they tender him a contract in hopes of getting a suitable return for him in a trade? Or do they talk to him, trust him, work with him and believe in him long term?
 Other Twins who are Arbitration-Eligible
 Will the Twins tender 2027 contracts to the following arbitration-eligible Twins players? Here they are shown with their projected 2027 contracts. I'll throw my two cents in on each player. 
 Joe Ryan ($9.6 million): Easy choice. Pick it up. Also, don't be afraid to see just how much trade value he might have. this offseason, with doubts about the 2027 season
 Bailey Ober ($6.9 million): He's been so solid, and such a team guy since he's been in the big leagues. Utmost respect for him doing as much as he has done while struggling to hit 90 the last couple of years. Explore trades all day, right to the last month. But definitely a non-tender candidate. 
 Dean Kremer ($6.5 Million): I miss Jhomardo Reyes, but I was wrong about Kremer. He came over from Baltimore and pitched quite well most of his Twins starts. Sits more around 92-94 and seems like a thinking person's pitcher. 
 Trevor Larnach ($6.3 million): Was putting up a very solid 2026 season until wrist injuries shut him down and he recently had surgery. Solid player, but the reality is it's a number game, and with the likes of Alan Roden, Walker Jenkins, Emmanuel Rodriguez, Hendry Mendez, the Twins have good left-handed outfield options. They also have Byron Buxton, Austin Martin, Luke Keaschall and Gabriel Gonzalez. Look to trade all day, but is a non-tender is possible.
 Cole Sands ($1.3 million): Tremendous out of the Twins bullpen in 2025 .2026 was filled with injuries for Sands. More difficult decision, especially as it appears a few starters may be pushed to the bullpen. 
 Tommy Nance ($1.2 million): came to the Twins ahead of the 2026 trade deadline. Easy tender.

 Below this paragraph is what I wrote on a board related to Lewis recently. I too have changed my mind. Call it a crappy hunch, but I could see Lewis being somewhat humbled by his 2026 campaign and adopting some different approaches.
 Lewis is on a minimal contract. He wasn't really good at third base but he was ok. He managed to pick up first base better than expected and was particularly good at scooping poor throws even as he struggled with the nuances of where to line up on relays or occasionally wandering too far off the bag on grounders to the second baseman. At the dish, Lewis has worn out his welcome with many because of his addiction to the low outside pitches, which he obstinately attempts to pull. The other side of the coin is that Lewis is not someone with high K rates, he can run a little bit, and the ball still comes off his bat in a sweet fashion. In various iterations of a roster, often I have dumped Lewis from the team. That has changed. 
 I'm now more inclined to hold him unless he returns real value. The only way Lewis returns value is if he is packaged with another player like Ryan. I don't see a good trade for Ryan so this leaves Royce at 1B if the Twins can bring in Brandon Lowe or 2B if the Twins choose to sign Ty France. Lewis will be a better defender than Clemens after he gets the repetitions he needs to learn the position because he is more athletic.
 While I never previously bought into the hype for Royce Lewis because I saw only an undisciplined player, I now see a rehabbing guy who may come into 2027 with his legs back to what can be his 100% health going forward. I also think he will finally adopt the approaches his coaches have brought to him about punishing those middle and middle high outside pitches to right field while laying off the outside worm borers. It could happen but I could be stone cold wrong too.

 All very interesting.  But the key question remains: where does Lewis play?
 He’s clearly not a good enough hitter to be the starting 1B or 2B on a team that has emphatically announced through its actions that they intend to compete vigorously in ‘27.  To slot Lewis in either of those positions hoping for some sort of miraculous turnaround would be self defeating.
 Moreover, what particular skill set does Lewis have that would warrant keeping him as a utility player, particularly under the contract terms suggested?  Speed, defensive ace, bat - to - ball skills, etc.? He’s not a standout in any area per se.
 And, to be honest, is he really a huge culture/glue guy?   Hmmm.
 The entire #1 pick rationale is water under the bridge as well.  Besides, the effort to justify that decision was has been made under a different regime and era. There’s a new sheriff and vibe in town now.
 With no place to play and new management in place, Lewis should welcome the opportunity for a new start elsewhere as opposed to just hanging on here struggling for innings with the failed top pick mantle hanging over his head.

 The Twins can't be run based on sentimentality. Bringing back Lewis at all is questionable but obviously nothing like Seth's idea here is even remotely on the table.

 Boy, I don't know. I'd love for it to work out with Royce, but he's been a bad hitter for 2 1/2 seasons now. During that time he might put together a hot streak that lasts a few weeks (at most), but it's always cancelled out by a dreadful run where he looks unplayable. 
 He was so bad last season he got demoted. Sure, he came right back up and had one of his hot stretches, but he was one of the prime examples why the Twins stumbled into oblivion down the stretch last season. How is he going to solve his issues at the plate where he's guessing at every pitch, flailing at pitches 2 feet outside the zone, and looking completely lost?
